key_facts: **Purpura** is bleeding into the skin that does **not blanch**: petechiae (<2 mm), purpura (2–10 mm), ecchymoses (>1 cm).
**Non-blanching rash in an unwell or febrile child: meningococcal sepsis until proven otherwise** (NICE NG240: benzylpenicillin, 999).
Flat purpura: platelets, clotting, vessel fragility (steroids, age, scurvy); palpable purpura: vasculitis.
Tests: FBC and film, clotting, U&E, LFT, CRP, blood cultures if febrile; urine and BP for vasculitis.
Consider leukaemia (petechiae, pallor, bone pain), ITP, anticoagulants and non-accidental injury in children.

rows: **Infants 4 months–2 years**: large **rosette/target/medallion purpuric plaques** on face, ears and limbs with oedema and fever, but **the child looks well**. Usually skin-only; resolves in 1–3 weeks
Cold-precipitating immunoglobulins (type II/III mixed — **hepatitis C**, Sjögren's, lymphoma; type I — myeloma/Waldenström's occlusion)
Adults; palpable purpura on legs, **acral necrosis/ulcers, livedo**, Raynaud's, arthralgia, neuropathy, **membranoproliferative GN**, low C4; DIF IgM ( option 5)

Rare in children; sinusitis, crusting, epistaxis, saddle nose, lung nodules/haemorrhage, **GN**; skin: palpable purpura, ulcers, nodules, **oral ulcers/"strawberry gums"**. Biopsy: **necrotising vasculitis with granulomas** ( option 2)
Autoantibody platelet destruction (often post-viral in children)
**Well child, flat petechiae and bruising, mucosal bleeding; platelets <100 (often <20) × 10⁹/L**; otherwise normal FBC/film. Most children recover in 6 months
*N. meningitidis* endotoxin → DIC and septic vasculitis

**Unwell, febrile child or young adult**; rapidly spreading **non-blanching petechiae → purpura fulminans**; cold peripheries, leg pain, abnormal colour, tachycardia, ± neck stiffness — a **999 emergency**

ul: **"The glass test is negative so it's fine"**: early meningococcal rash may blanch; judge the whole child.

sections.title: Pathophysiology and pathology
blocks: Purpura means **red cells outside vessels**: from low platelets, clotting defects, fragile or inflamed vessels.

mech.t: Low or dysfunctional platelets cause petechiae and mucosal bleeding.
Clotting factor deficiency causes larger bruises and deep bleeds.
Thin dermis (age, steroids) or weak collagen (scurvy) lets vessels tear: senile purpura.
Inflamed vessels leak red cells, causing raised palpable purpura.
mech.caption: Vasculitis: neutrophils damage small vessels and red cells leak into the dermis.

sections.title: Diagnosis and investigations
blocks: FBC + film (platelets), clotting/D-dimer/fibrinogen (DIC), blood cultures/meningococcal PCR, ANCA, cryoglobulins (37 °C), HCV, C3/C4, urinalysis.

sections.title: Differential diagnoses
blocks: Also: non-accidental injury, Henoch–Schönlein purpura (see *IgA vasculitis*), leukaemia, haemophilia/von Willebrand, scurvy, HUS, drug-induced thrombocytopenia (heparin, quinine, valproate, co-trimoxazole).

sections.title: Management
blocks: **NICE NG240:** in suspected meningococcal disease, transfer immediately to hospital; give **parenteral benzylpenicillin** (or ceftriaxone/cefotaxime) at the earliest opportunity **if it will not delay transfer**. Doses: benzylpenicillin IM/IV — **adults and children ≥10 years 1.2 g; 1–9 years 600 mg; <1 year 300 mg** (check BNF/BNFC). Many community IP settings will not hold it — call 999.

refer.t: Unwell with a non-blanching rash: **999**, benzylpenicillin if there will be a delay (NICE NG240).
Petechiae with pallor, lymph nodes, bone pain or bruising: **same-day FBC and film** (leukaemia, ITP).

sections.title: Red flags and when to refer

ul: Unwell with a non-blanching rash: **999**, benzylpenicillin if there will be a delay (NICE NG240).
Petechiae with pallor, lymph nodes, bone pain or bruising: **same-day FBC and film** (leukaemia, ITP).

blocks: Any non-blanching rash in an unwell or febrile patient → 999. Purpura + low platelets → same-day haematology. Purpura + sinus/lung/renal symptoms or positive ANCA → urgent rheumatology/renal.

ul: Depends on cause: sepsis, haemorrhage, organ damage.

pearls: Teach parents the **glass/tumbler test**, but stress that an **unwell child needs urgent help even if the rash blanches**.

quiz.q: When should you think of Purpura: the differential diagnosis?
quiz.a: Non-blanching red or purple spots or bruises, in a child or an adult.
Low or faulty platelets, clotting problems, fragile vessels (age, steroids, scurvy) or vessel inflammation.

quiz.q: What is the backbone of care?
quiz.a: Glass test; is the patient unwell? FBC and film, clotting, U&E, LFT, CRP, urine; same-day if unwell or platelets low.
Meningococcal sepsis, leukaemia, ITP, DIC, cryoglobulinaemic or ANCA vasculitis, non-accidental injury.

quiz.q: Name a red flag that needs escalation.
quiz.a: Unwell with a non-blanching rash: **999**, benzylpenicillin if there will be a delay (NICE NG240).
